cards.front: Recall a key point about Harmony and Tonality
cards.back: Consonant harmony sounds stable and restful; dissonant harmony sounds tense and unresolved — both are deliberate compositional choices.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Harmony and Tonality
cards.back: Cadences are harmonic endings: perfect (V-I, final), plagal (IV-I, amen), imperfect (I-V or IV-V, unfinished), interrupted (V-vi, surprise).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Harmony and Tonality
cards.back: Modulation changes the key centre: to the dominant (5th scale degree), subdominant (4th), or relative major/minor — each creates a different shift of mood.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Harmony and Tonality
cards.back: Pedal notes are sustained or repeated while harmony changes above them — dominant pedals build tension; tonic pedals create stability.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Name cadences by TYPE (perfect, plagal, imperfect, interrupted). Use Roman numerals for chord analysis. Identify modulations and their destination keys. Explain the emotional effect of harmonic choices.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: A cadence is just the end of a piece. Correct: A cadence is a harmonic PROGRESSION at the end of a phrase, not necessarily the end of a piece. There are four main types (perfect, plagal, imperfect, interrupted) each with a distinct sound and function. Identifying cadences by TYPE is essential for the exam.
Identify and name the cadences in a piece you have studied. Explain how each cadence contributes to the structure and emotional direction of the music.

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Harmony and Tonality
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Show knowledge of Harmony and Tonality using appropriate musical vocabulary (e.g. terminology for elements, devices, and contexts).

Harmony and Tonality is a key element of GCSE Music requiring theoretical understanding and practical application. The AQA specification requires you to identify, describe and analyse this element in set works and unfamiliar music. cards.front: Applying Harmony and Tonality in Performance and Composition
cards.back: Understanding harmony and tonality informs your performing (AO1) and composing (AO2) work. In performance, awareness of harmony and tonality helps you make interpretive decisions that serve the music. In composition, harmony and tonality provides the building blocks of your creative work — the choices you make about this element shape the identity and coherence of your piece.

cards.front: Exam Technique for Harmony and Tonality Questions
cards.back: In the AQA GCSE Music listening exam, questions about harmony and tonality typically ask you to: identify features by ear; describe how they are used; explain their effect; compare features between extracts. The key to success is precise terminology — never use vague language.
